questions.problem:
Which of the following matrices are symmetric?

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & \frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{1}{2} & 1\end{aligned}],\,Q=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,R=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal. 

With that in mind, let's examine each matrix in turn.

- $P$ is a symmetric matrix. Indeed, $P={P}^{T}.$

- $Q$ is *not* a symmetric matrix. Since ${q}_{23}\ne {q}_{32},$ we obtain $Q\ne {Q}^{T}.$

$$
Q=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

- $R$ is *not* a symmetric matrix. Since ${r}_{12}\ne {r}_{21},$ we obtain $R\ne {R}^{T}.$

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$P$ only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- If $A$ is symmetric, then ${A}^{-1}$ is always symmetric (if it exists).
- The sum of *any* two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric.
- If $A$ is *any*  $n\times n$ matrix, then ${A}^{T}A$ is always symmetric.
questions.worked_solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any non-singular symmetric matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}({A}^{-1})^{T} & =({A}^{T})^{-1} \\  & ={A}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+B)^{T} & ={A}^{T}+{B}^{T} \\  & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}({A}^{T}A)^{T} & ={A}^{T}({A}^{T})^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true? 

- If $A$ is *any* matrix, then ${A}^{3}$ is always symmetric.
- The sum of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric.
- The difference of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric.
questions.worked_solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. As a counterexample, consider the matrix 

$\,$ $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].$

However, ${A}^{3}$ is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3} & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+B)^{T} & ={A}^{T}+{B}^{T} \\  & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-B)^{T} & ={A}^{T}-{B}^{T} \\  & =A-B.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

$$

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- If $A$ is *any*  $n\times n$  matrix, then $A-{A}^{T}$ is always symmetric.
- The sum of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric.
- If $A$ is symmetric, then ${A}^{-1}$ is always symmetric (if it exists).
questions.worked_solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. As a counterexample, consider the matrix 

$\,$ $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].$

However, $A-{A}^{T}$ is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{A}^{T} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+B)^{T} & ={A}^{T}+{B}^{T} \\  & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any non-singular symmetric matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}({A}^{-1})^{T} & =({A}^{T})^{-1} \\  & ={A}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- The product of two $n\times n$ diagonal matrices is always symmetric.
- If $A$ is *any* $n\times n$ matrix, then ${A}^{2}$ is always symmetric.
- If $A$ is *any*  $n\times n$ matrix, then $A+{A}^{T}$ is always symmetric.
questions.worked_solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any diagonal matrices $A$ and $B,$ their product $AB$ is also diagonal, and any diagonal matrix is symmetric.

- Statement II is false. As a counterexample, consider the matrix 

$\,$ $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}].$

However, ${A}^{2}$ is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any square matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+{A}^{T})^{T} & ={A}^{T}+({A}^{T})^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}+A \\  & =A+{A}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."
